Crysis is a classic title and in my opinion one of the 5 greatest FPS games of all time. The look, the sounds, the feel, the story, the game-play. EVERYTHING is awesome about this game.

Why not buy it on Steam then? No disrespect to Steam as I LOVE Steam! However, this title originally shipped on disc which is where I spent hundreds of hours of my time while in college. The disc version included a 64-bit version of the executable. This Steam version of the game does NOT include the 64-bit version of that executable file. There are ways to modify the game files to get it working however not only is it not recommended for novices it simply isn't desirable having to go through that much trouble for a game that has DRM which limits number of installations.

Instead, do yourself a favor and get the version of this game sold on GOG.com which does NOT limit your number of installations as that version includes NO DRM WHATSOEVER. Also, that version includes the missing 64-bit version of the game.

Why is that 64-bit version of the game so important? This title was one of the first made to support Direct X 10 when Windows Vista was terrorizing the populace. The 32-bit version of the game, especially with mods or maxed out settings, runs terribly due to poor optimization. Even if you use a 4GB patch on the 32-bit executable the game will continue to run like garbage.

On the 64-bit executable you can run the game flawlessly on modern systems and experience one of the greatest FPS titles of our time. This game is incredibly fun. Go to GOG.com and pick it up cheap!

EDIT: I forgot to mention one thing about this game. For some odd reason Crysis will not run properly at 60fps when playing at 1920x1080. If you play on a TV the game will lock to the cinema mode at 24fps which is game breaking. If you play on a normal computer monitor it will still screw up and lock itself to about 50fps.
There are two ways to get around this...
A) Lower your resolution to something else. 1680x1050 works fine for me.
B) Create a custom resolution with your GPU's control panel of 1904x1071 (1920x1080 minus 16x9). This is literally the next step down from 1080p so it is so close that the game looks the same yet it tricks your TV/monitor into running at 60fps.
Crysis 2 has this same dang problem and so does the original Rome:Total War.
Crysis 1 was one of the best games ever produced and way ahead of its time. Story is solid This game in 2007 was better than Battlefield from Dice has ever been.

From what I understand, Steam and EA could never get their shit together and so when you download and install the game you receive files meant for the 32bit version of the game. What you have to then do is download the files for the 64bit version, rename them to the name for the 32bit files and delete the 32bit files. I don't have a super high end PC but according to the minimum specs I should've been able to run it decently on medium settings. So I start the game, and I'm getting a pretty consistent frame rate, but every 10-15 minutes of gameplay the game crashes for absolutely no reason and you have to restart it. This got very annoying, very quickly. So I found another fix, what you can do is go to your steam library, right click Crysis, hit properties, general, set launch parameters and type in "-dx9" This runs the game in direct X 9 instead of 10 to further performance. Doing this solved that issue, and I was able to play the game worry free for a couple of hours. Now it's crashing again for a new reason and I don't know why. How steam can sell a game that is essentially broken on the marketplace is beyond me. When I buy a game, I expect to be able to install, and enjoy it with little issue. This game has been one headache after another and it sucks because when the game works I absolutely love it.

I’m almost surprised we don’t still talk about Crysis regularly when discussing first-person shooters. Not all games age gracefully but this is one of the few that you could argue has grown better with age, because technology eventually caught up to the insane graphical abilities folded into this thing. It may be more than ten years old but it looks better than plenty of games that have released in the last year, and has more open-ended gameplay to boot. But there is ultimately a reason Crysis doesn’t often come up in conversation despite its strengths, and it’s a pretty big one.

Crysis was ahead of its time in a lot of ways, such as blaming the Koreans for everything. Yes, the dastardly North Koreans found something on a Pacific island that could spell doom for the world, so the U.S. has deployed a small squad of soldiers to the area, armed with top-secret nanosuits. These fibrous contraptions can grant super speed or strength, armor or invisibility, making the wearer the perfect covert engine of war. The mission doesn’t go at all as planned, however, and you’ve got to scramble to find out what’s going on and how you can stop it before your foes make a very, very big mistake.

At its heart this is an open-world shooter, much in the vein of Far Cry before it. The maps for your missions are vast, fully-modeled tracts of island, giving you plenty of cliffs and jungle to forge through if you want routes around checkpoints or towns. Unlike Far Cry though, your nanosuit actually gives you powerful options for approaching your challenges. Armor gives you enough health to take serious hits while gunning down whole squads, speed lets you tear through the jungle or run right up on hapless troops, invisibility allows you to ghost past entire sections of the map, and strength makes you leap high enough to ignore fences and cliffs. Combined with a rapidly-recharging power reserve, you can vary up your tactics on a whim to gun down one outpost of foes and then sneak through an entire town undetected.

Crysis ends up feeling like a more complete experience because of these choices available to the player, on top of the excellent gunplay. Your weapons feel weighty and powerful, from silenced pistols all the way up to guided missile launchers. You’ll be challenged to take down tanks and helicopters and even tougher foes as you progress so don’t expect to stealth through the entire game, but traversing the vast maps definitely gives you plenty of leeway to do as you please. You’ll have vehicles to commandeer as well, ultimately giving the game a similar feel to the later Far Cry games but with a more structured, military edge.

And honestly that might be what holds this one back. Crysis is a military shooter at its core, despite the sci-fi elements and open maps. You’re always going to be following orders to clear checkpoints or raid field bases for intel or secure landing sites. The maps give you the latitude to navigate and plan as you please but only for the purposes of fulfilling your mission, not turning up secrets or completing side activities. For most people this is still probably enough and I’ve enjoyed my time with the game, but whenever I hit a rough fight that I have to try a few times I feel more ready to leave this one behind than I do with most shooters.

Regardless of that though, Crysis is something that needs to be seen to be appreciated. The technological achievements are undeniable, offering realistic characters that move and emote with striking clarity and island vistas that could have come from a postcard. The action is plenty capable of keeping up, and the options afforded by your nanosuit add a remarkable amount of depth to the gameplay. Whatever your feelings on military shooters you owe it to yourself to check this one out, just to see what can be accomplished with the right thinking towards the future. Crysis remains a polished gem even ten years out, perhaps a bit simple in structure but no less beautiful for it.

All the way back in 2009, the first Crysis got a lot of attention for its graphics. On one hand, the game got praise for being visually stunning. On the other hand, it got flak for being a glorified tech demo that could barely run on anyone's machine, kickstarting the meme "but can it run Crysis?" 

It's 2018 now, a lot of games look this good, and Crysis runs fine, so all that is ancient history. 

Crysis 2 and 3, released shortly afterwards, got reputations for being generic, pretty, streamlined CoD-ish hallway shooters. 

But the first Crysis is a very different game from its sequels. 

Crysis wasn't mindblowing, but it's an interesting vision of a very freeform, systems and AI-driven, not-quite-open-world-but-very-open FPS game. It's got a lot going for it. It makes you feel like a jungle predator. It gives you more real problem-solving freedom than Far Cry. Challenges come from AI flanking you, laying down covering fire, and flushing you out with grenades, not mobbing you. The suit is super cool and energy management is a good mechanic. The hardest difficulty even makes enemies speak in Korean. If you're looking for an exciting story-driven cinematic shooter, you're probably going to be disappointed. But it's a well-designed jungle adventure that has you playing an invisible supersolder who tosses chickens at Koreans, and that's worth something.

I remember when this game first came out and no one could run it. Several people I knew went out and got new graphics cards that day. What got it working for me:

METHOD 1)

Download Crysis Warhead. You have to have it for the Bin64 folder. 

For Crysis Warhead:
1) Download Both Crysis & Crysis Warhead
2) Open the folder where Crysis Warhead is installed
3) You'll see a Bin32 folder and a Bin64 folder
4) Delete the Bin32 folder
5) Rename the Bin64 folder to Bin32
6) Open the new Bin32 folder
7) Delete the "Crysis" application
8) Rename the "Crysis64" application to just "Crysis"
9) Crysis Warhead Now Works!

For Crysis:
1) Right click and copy that new Bin32 folder you made for Crysis Warhead
2) Paste it into the Crysis install file (replace the old "Bin32" file with the new one from Crysis Warhead.
3) Crysis Now Works!

This game is well-known for being beautiful, but to desribe it only as eye candy really sells Crysis short.  There's a lot to enjoy about the gameplay, especially how it breaks up the old "series of chest-high-walls" shooter formula.

As a super soldier your suit contains a variety of powers that can be toggled between:  super strength (enhancing melee abilities), super speed, maximum armor, and active camouflage (which makes you truly invisible to enemies who haven't seen you yet).  Active camo is the true selling point, learning to use it (and honestly, abuse it) is what keeps you alive.  Your character is not well suited for going in guns blazing, you'll rely on stealth and run-and-gun tactics against enemies who prefer to hunt you instead of bunkering down behind a chest high wall.  In general, human enemy AI is fantastic and pushes you to quickly learn how to survive a Crysis fire-fight.

Weapons customization is another well-done aspect of Crysis.  The same gun can be customized to a short/medium range spray-and-pray style semi-automatic, or a long-range silenced sniper with a scope and laser sight, all pretty much on-the-fly.  So while the number of unique weapons is actually pretty small (5 or 6 maybe), you can get a lot more mileage out of them through customization.  

While the first stretch of the game fighting human enemies is very fun, the game has an abrupt change when you begin to encounter mostly aliens.  I definitely found this part much less enjoyable, it seems more about showing what you can do with the Cry Engine than keeping the game fun for the player.  My level of interest dropped off pretty sharply, to the extent that I didn't even finish the game.
That doesn't mean I'm not glad I bought it (I definitely still recommened it), and you may not have the same experience I had.

This is the version you want, not Crysis Remastered.

Remastered is based on the console version of Crysis.  They enhanced some things, like texture quality, but broke everything else.  The new lighting engine looks horrible, the dynamic physics are greatly simplified, and an entire level is missing.

Unfortunately, this original version of the game has been ignored and doesn't run well on modern OSes.  Luckily users have fixed this.  Look for "c1 launcher" on Github and follow the instructions to get it working.

It took me a while to be fond of this game as I played it years ago and while my rig met the minimum requirements (almost reached the recommended ones) it had a hard time running Crysis on it properly. There were numerous glitches, audio issues and frequent CTDs.

But you know what? Putting the technical difficulties aside this is a damn fine game! You play Nomad, a special forces soldier who wears a so-called nanosuit. The story takes place in the future and the objective is to find out what happened on the island previously seized by Koreans. 

While you traverse through the deep jungle and small settlements you notice two things: the game is stunningly beautiful (there was a reason for the high system reqs) and that by hiding-shooting you cannot eliminate your foes. You need to utilise your nanosuit. 

You can bring up a special menu and select from various abilities. Speed makes you faster, Strength allows you to melee your foes or throw bigger objects and Stealth makes you invisible. All drain your energy bar (which will refill automatically, but slowly) and I do not have to mention that Stealth is the most exciting and most useful among all. Oh, yes, there's a 4th power enabling you to take more damage.

Enemy AI is great - they respond to the noises, work in squads and will try to find you even if you are invisible. On greater difficulty settings they speak Korean so you do not understand what commands they give to one another.

Occasionally, the game throws in some scripted cutscenes - these look good and also interesting. By looking at the pictures on the store page one can guess what they'll find (and what the army was really looking into), but let's not spoil it here.

Crysis is a stunningly beautiful game (even today considering it's more than 5 years old) and makes for an interesting, action-packed ride.

[h1][b]Introduction[/b][/h1]
When [b]Crysis[/b] released back in 2007, I did not know much about it, as I did not care about new releases at all. However, the strange, advanced looking suit on the box caught my eye, and I had to get it as soon as possible. It turned out that I could not even launch the game, as my graphic card was too weak. [i]“But Can It Run Crysis?”[/i] was a popular joke among the community, but for me, it was a harsh reality. However, once I was able to play it, I immediately fell in love with its visual presentation, gripping campaign, and fascinating multiplayer. The question is if [b]Crysis[/b] can still hold up to this day? It certainly can, but it has its shortcomings.
[h3][b]Story[/b][/h3]
An American team of archeologists discovers ancient alien machines on Linghsan Island. However, North Koreans capture them shortly after the discovery, and they cut off the islands from the rest of the world. You play as [b]Nomad[/b], a member of the dispatched [b]Raptor Team[/b], who wears a technologically advanced [b]Nanosuit[/b], which gives him superhuman abilities, such as invisibility or strength. Your task is to evacuate the archeologists and secure any valuable information. Once you get onto the island, you find out that some of these machines are still functional and not that happy with your presence, so they turn small skirmishes between Americans and Koreans into a massive slaughterhouse.

While the game’s plot is serviceable and a bit intriguing from the start, it does not have any interesting characters. The North Korean antagonist is forgettable, and your fellow team members are no better, as there is no depth or proper character development. And that is a shame as the game occasionally forces [b]Nomad[/b] into interaction with them, yet I have not managed to care about them at all. The positive aspect is that the story does not pretend to be smarter than it actually is, and it does not interrupt you from gameplay. Its narrative is simply about a group of American soldiers fighting Koreans and Aliens, and that is enough for this kind of game.
[h3][b]Gameplay[/b][/h3]
To my surprise, I still enjoyed the twelve hours long campaign a lot. The game has several levels, and most of them are pretty open, which allows you to choose a path and style that suits you, as the game only shows you your objective on the map. There are occasional side objectives, which can either help you with your mission or give you additional information about the story. You will go through dense jungles, beautiful beaches, rocky mountains, vast plains, and several industrial complexes, so the levels are pretty varied. That variety is one of the reasons I enjoyed replaying the game so much, as each mission is different and offers something new and unique. There is not much time for sightseeing, though, as Koreans have a lot of military camps and patrols in the area, and they also can call for reinforcements.

You can use vehicles to travel through these open locations. Several civilian cars are drivable, as well as Humvees, military trucks, and even tanks. You are not limited only to ground vehicles, as you can use boats and even pilot a VTOL in one mission. All vehicles are easy to control, and using them against your enemies is both advantageous and enjoyable.

As mentioned before, you are wearing an advanced [b]Nanosuit[/b], which makes you more effective in combat. You have four [b]Nanosuit[/b] modes to choose from: an armour, which makes you more resistant to damage; invisibility for stealthy approach; strength for higher jumps, bashing through the walls, and picking up and throwing heavy objects; and speed for your overall movement and weapon handling. Those abilities draw power from your suit’s energy, which recharges after a while. Switching suit’s mods often is essential, and changing your position in a blink of an eye while causing mayhem among Koreans is just entertaining.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2227878313
Your weapon arsenal is pretty standard for this genre, as there are a few assault rifles, shotgun, submachine gun, as well as few interesting pieces, such as minigun or Gauss rifle. Lethal grenades, rocket launchers, or flashbangs and smoke grenades are present too. What makes [b]Crysis[/b] a bit unique is its weapon customization, where you can add several attachments without pausing the game. That is a feature I wish was more common today. You can find weapon attachments at enemies or their camps.

As there are quite a lot of explosives, you might be asking if the environment is destructible. Well, partially. A lot of enemy towers, bunkers, and civilian shacks are destroyable, and their debris might hurt or kill your enemies. Unfortunately, some buildings might be destroyable only via a scripted event or not at all. However, grabbing poor Korean by the neck and throwing him against obstacles is satisfying enough to make it up for it.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2227912178
Your enemies consist mostly of Korean soldiers, who will use every abovementioned equipment and vehicles against you. I must say that I still had a lot of fun fighting them, as they are pretty aggressive and try to use the environment to their advantage a bit. Of course, their AI is a bit outdated for today’s standard, so you can sometimes confuse them if you spam explosives in their camp or shoot at them from hundreds of meters, even on the highest difficulty setting.

Another part of the game is fighting against the aliens. That is different than fighting with Koreans, as they have an octopus-like appearance, and their movement is pretty fast and a bit unpredictable. There are several types of aliens, from small ones who can jump several meters away, to bigger ones, which fly around the sky. There are also a few bosses. However, as much as I like that fighting them feels different and requires a different strategy than with Koreans, I do not like that the whole game becomes a lot more linear once aliens become regular enemies. While the first half of the game shows me all the possibilities and says: do whatever you want; the second half of the game strips that off and says: go straight and shoot. [h1]NOTE:[/h1] I originally finished the game using my disc based copy of the game bought in 2007. I bought it again on steam because it was included in the Crysis Franchise Pack.

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
One of the rare PC Exclusive titles to break free from the Console's restrictive and dated hardware. Crysis 1 was the benchmark for most PC games back in 2007 until it was finally replaced by Metro 2033 in 2010.

Crysis follows the story of Jake "Nomad" Dunn, member of a Delta Ops Nano Team tasked with infiltrating an Island currently occupied by North Korean Forces. Not soon after landing, the Delta team finds out that the KPA is the least of their worries.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Cutting Edge Graphics: -Considering this game was released in 2007, Crysis can still go toe-to-toe with the 2012 game Far Cry 3. Back then, almost 95% of all PCs in the world could not run Crysis on its maximum settings. Crysis 1 was meant to be a PC only exclusive mostly because the developers really wanted to push both their creative freedom and raw hardware power. This is the game also spawned the internet meme: "But can it run Crysis?"

+ Innovative Gameplay: -This game was the first to introduce the Nano Suit which added a wide variety of new approaches to missions and objectives. A Quick hand and good reflexes are needed to fully utilize the Nano Suit's power.

+ Pseudo Open World: -Its not Sandbox, but it's not linear. Each mission objective involves a map of gigantic proportions where you can go and carefully plan out your strategy before going in a mission. Like what I said in my SW: Republic Commando Review, not every game needs to be sandbox. Crysis 1 had a good style by giving enough freedom while keeping the player in a directed flow in the story.

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- Terrible Optimization: -Although it was the Graphical Flagship of its time, the devs mainly focused on sheer brute force power of the GPU but made so little optimization. If properly optimized, most mid-range PCs could have ran this game a bit better.

- Unresolved Bugs: -6 years and some of the bugs from the first release still persists. Downloading some of the latest patches actually causes a bug. Not game breaking but terribly annoying.

- Resolution Problem: -You may or may not encounter this problem but the game seems to have a problem doing a full screen with a 1920x1080 resolution. To fix this, you'll need to edit the settings via note pad.

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
MUST HAVE. One of the landmark games that dared a primarily Console dominated market to shine a great light once more to the PC.

Additional Note: This is not a fast paced action game like COD or Battlefield. This game actually requires some planning and tactical movements to get the job done, specially in some of the harder difficulties.

Do you miss first person action games like GoldenEye, Thief 2, and the original Ghost Recon? If you miss games that simply put you in an environment, gave you some objectives, and let you figure out how to do them without driving you down a rollercoaster, the original Crysis is arguably the last and most technically advanced game of this type to be developed. The visual achievements of the CryEngine have overshadowed the fact that this game, well most of it at least, is a shining example of objective-based game design released just before everyone took shooters in the complete opposite direction.

The first level, which is shown off in the demo that’s available at crysisdemo.com as of this writing, is a perfect example of this. In a small bay occupied by a few enemy fortifications along the shore and some motorboat patrols, Crysis gives you two main objectives and an optional objective to tackle in any order. You can work your way along the coastline through the forts, take over a boat to zip around the bay, or whatever, through any combination of stealth and assault tactics.

This continues through the next several levels which are sort of a linear chain of small sandboxes: a village you can infiltrate from multiple angles, a group of bases along a river, a harbor, and so-on. The level design in all these areas is quite good, always giving you options and setups for fire fights that never happen the same way twice. This is even true in the game’s more linear sections early on. In the early parts (more on that later), even when Crysis is a corridor it’s still a very wide corridor.

I think the best way to describe the core game mechanics would be to call Crysis a simulation based on the original 1987 Predator movie. Your tools are Schwarzenegger-esque explosions and futuristic super powers. The nanosuit let’s you choose between super armor (the default), increased running speed, and a temporary stealth cloak. You’ll probably use the cloak the most but the other powers offer potential for fun combinations and interesting choices. Super strength let’s you jump higher, and you can combine it with speed for running super jumps. When sniping you can choose between staying hidden with the cloak or using strength for a more stable shooting arm.

Behind the nanosuit the Crysis boasts a varied sandbox of shooter mechanics. Not only is there the ever-present option of stealth, but you can also lift and throw most objects at enemies and control various vehicles. Most buildings in the game are also dynamically destructible through the physics engine, which feels like it has a tangible effect on gameplay. Crysis even let’s you fit most weapons with a modest variety of attachments with a quick tap of the C key like different sights or a silencer.

The reason you might hear a lot of people praise Crysis by saying “the first half” or “the first two thirds” of the game, is because for some reason it turns into a different, much worse game at a specific point later on. The later sections of Crysis are far more linear and introduce gameplay mechanics that while unique, just don’t work that well.  It’s probably best if you stop playing when you start a boss fight with a North Korean general. The most succinct thing I can say is at that point it feels like the level designers ran out of gas.

The good parts of Crysis though will still net you at least around 10 hours of gameplay, and that’s just for one run. I consider Crysis to be a pretty replayable game just because you can approach its missions with multiple strategies, but also because each difficulty mode above normal changes things considerably.

On normal you can pretty much toy with enemies using the nanosuit. On hard you can still play with them a little bit, but you have to be smart about it. Higher difficulties change a few core mechanics, and the deadlier enemies ensure you have to rethink the way you use the cloak and cover. Hard and Delta mode almost turn Crysis into a straight-up stealth game.

Of course what Crysis is most well-known for is the “but can it run Crysis?” joke pertaining to the game’s harsh treatment of processors. Even after six years, Crysis is not an extremely easy game to run. My GTX 760 still only get’s 60 frames per second MOST of the time in 1080p. The consumer experience when you first install the game doesn’t make things easier either.

Being from the early days of DirectX 10, Crysis forces it on you by artificially locking the highest graphics features behind DX10 when they are in fact available on DX9 just by editing the ini file or downloading a custom one. DX10 does little more than drag down performance of the already demanding Crysis.

If you’re wondering if Crysis still holds up visually after six years, I think with vanilla settings it’s beginning to show its age, but still looks significantly better than most console games released in even the last couple years. Really, only the highest-end recent PC games (Crysis 3, Metro, Battlefield 4), and next-gen-console-only launch games like Killzone Shadow Fall beat it. It can still look impressive with custom ini files and texture packs though.

I think it’s kind of a crime Crysis got labled as just “that really pretty PC game nobody can run.” In my opinion it’s one of the most underrated first person shooters of this past console generation (it did come out on consoles eventually after all), if not one of the best. It’s one of the last, if not the last of a breed of shooter that game designers seemingly forgot in the chase after Call of Duty’s popularity.

[h1] Crysis Review [/h1]

Simply put, Crysis is an absolute beast of a game. Even now 14 years on from its original release it's going to give your PC a run for its money due to Crytek’s assumption that the future of CPU design was clock speeds and not the amount of cores; spoiler alert, they guessed wrong. However, it is still objectively easier to run these days after years of hardware progression and is probably one of the nicest looking games around. CryEngine 2 had a lot to showcase here with character models and facial animations only rivalled at the time by Source and breathtaking landscapes filled with sandy beaches, crop fields and dense jungles complimented by some impressive volumetric lighting. But enough about graphics, what’s it about and more importantly how does it play?

Upon starting the campaign you are put into the boots of Nomad - a charisma vacuum - I mean a US special forces soldier with access to a high-tech nanosuit that enhances the user's speed, strength, stealth and armour capabilities. Nomad and his squad are on a covert operation to rescue civilians and researchers from a South Pacific island that has been invaded by the North Koreans due to the discovery of ancient, alien technology. It’s a simple premise that starts off with a promising, tension-filled beginning but ends up being handled with as much nuance as a Call of Duty campaign.

The game's missions and set pieces also suffer from late game deterioration as the last third fails to live up to the quality of what came before. This is exemplified by the slow, meandering crawl through the alien’s homebase which goes on for far too long as you make your way through a zero-gravity cave system which is confusing to navigate and veers into frustration as you're hit with wave after wave of enemies. This is in stark contrast to the variety of missions that precede it that see Nomad behind enemy lines sabotaging vital communications equipment, destroying anti-air guns whilst US forces prepare their chaotic offensive and the actual assault on the North Korean troops as you roll on them with a company of tanks.

Now the biggest problem that Crysis faces is the marriage of its mechanics and level design which never quite coalesces, despite so much promise. You are given all the tools you’ll need from the very beginning (there are no skill trees or extra powers here) and dropped into the world to experiment and build up familiarity with Nomad’s powers until you become the super-soldier you dreamed of as a child, bashing Action Men into one another. The level design just doesn’t quite compliment these powers enough though. The maps are like sandboxes with alternate routes, secret paths and an emphasis on verticality which aids your covert sleuthing through the jungle but often falls apart in more open areas and the soldiers' encampments. These sections sometimes fall into generic cover shooting, especially on the higher difficulties, and often made me question why I had the powers to begin with - an issue that the expandalone Crysis: Warhead solved thankfully.

I have heard Crysis described as a glorified tech-demo that exudes style over substance and whilst that may be a little unfair it is understandable given the design of the game. The developers clearly wanted to create a power fantasy that allows the player to creatively use the tools and weapons at their disposal but they didn’t facilitate this enough through level design. Sure, the story may read like a US sanctioned propaganda piece and many facets of its design are inconsistent at best and painfully boring at worst. But all in all, Crysis does stand on its own as a relic of mid 2000’s PC gaming; a good game that couldn’t quite climb that hurdle to greatness but gosh, doesn’t it still look so pretty?

Crysis. A game Developed by Crytek and Published by Electronic Arts.

There was a time that Crysis was the be all and end all of PC crushing games. It was an incredibly resource hungry game, when PC's especially mid tier PC's didn't have a lot of resources to spare. This game was build only for the highest of end PC's and thusly wasn't enjoyed and experienced by a lot back at its release in 2007. Still however, as a PC killer, this game built it's notoriety and became an almost immediate cult classic by its fan base, for upping the quality of FPS games as a whole with improved physix, adaptation and exploration on a grand scale.

Story: 6/10
Purely based on the content of Crysis alone, not including Warhead which closes the chapter off properly. This game doesn't really provide any meat in terms of story till about 3/4 the way through it. The year is 2020 and you play as "Nomad" a special ops soldier garbed in cutting edge nano suit equipment, sent to the Lingshan Island to investigate the capture of a lead scientist who uncovered something in the South China Sea, and ultimately set them free. Upon first stepping foot on the Island you start upon you're beset upon a creature that starts picking off your team one by one. It is your job now not only to free the science team but eradicate whatever has been ripping apart Raptor team. A fairly standard FPS story to be fair, Not a lot of depth in its experience till previously mentioned later in the story. But not a bad experience as a whole just a bit over done and cliche.

Gameplay: 7/10
I'm trying to give Crysis the credit it is due, A lot of what is done here, isn't great by today's standards by any stretch of the imagination. But for it's time this would have been revolutionary. From the overall physix engine in place, to the specialising equipment and activating suit powers to adapt to the situation, most of that hadn't been experienced till this point.
Exploration: The islands are huge, This isn't a open world game though. You don't have free access to the entire landscape you are running around on, conveniently placed non-scaleable cliff faces litter the island to ensure you don't go too far off course. There is however a lot of room for exploring still. The game is quite linear in its design but there is quite a lot of space within those linear lines.
Gunplay: Probably the bread and butter of an FPS. Unfortunately however not the greatest experience here. Weapons feel heavy as they should, shooting things feels like it would hurt, However the ultimate mechanic of actually trying to navigate through the clunky controls is tedious at best. A lot of what we take for granted now, obviously had to be trial and error fixed over time. Perhaps this is where, or maybe it was just an oversight.
Controls: Stepping into the controls. The controls are clunky and it definitely pulls away from the experience as a whole. You expect a game that requires you to quickly transition between suit upgrades, and weapon modifications to at least be able to do it seamlessly, Instead you are given an experience that attempts to do it swiftly but a lot of the gameplay mechanics get in the way, For instance, aiming down the sights, you would assume iron sighting would be dropped when trying to sprint or activate other suit powers. This is not the case however, you can't do anything while you are actively toggled into aiming and obvious flaw from my perspective but again, at the time this may have been common standard...except that i don't recollect this mechanic in any other FPS game.
Suit Modifications: Probably what makes Crysis, Crysis. The suit modifications you can activate to control the situation. A great concept, except for the fact your suit apparently runs on AA batteries and has the capability of only activating an increase for an extremely limited time. You do feel like quite a bad ass when you are cloaking around the world and picking off enemies however or even sprinting into combat at unfathomable speeds. It has it's place but overall feels like a gimmick, You can quite happily and easily move throughout the game without activating any powers at all. The selection wheel feels like it should slow down time when accessing it giving you the illusion of instant transition and also the ability to exist in the forms for longer would definitely be an ideal trait here. Being able to run fast for 3 seconds or strength for 2 throws/3 jumps doesn't feel like much of a "power" rather a hindrance.

Visuals: 9/10
Again. Trying to throw Crysis a bone here because its more than 10 years old and at the time was probably the absolute pinnacle of graphical power and presence. Unfortunately i do have to mention that the base game doesn't have any resolutions beyond 1080p. This isn't a huge issue but playing on a standard 2K monitor you are experiencing the game in a rather blurry state, taking away from a lot of what made this game a power house. However playing this game on a mid - high range PC had absolutely no concerns running at all. Smooth as glass and absolutely no graphical concerns at all while exploring the island. Testament to a well design game for sure.


Audio: 8/10
Again, another bone based on its age and what it offered at its time of birth, Crysis definitely has some beautiful audio in place, you don't place it by today's standards with games being significantly larger in both scale and file size. But the audio here is quite well done, from the crunching of leaves under your feet to the splashing over water crashing against the shore, Crytek have definitely put a lot of love into the Crysis series for sure, and it's evident in almost every piece of its atmosphere. There however isn't much in place of "Soundtrack" nothing here captivated me musically which was a bit of a shame but as a whole the experience here was great.

Let's get to the actual review:
I played this game 9 years ago when it came out and I loved it. The Physics are some of the best I've seen in any game to date. You can destroy entire huts. Without having them collapse in a predetermined way. but instead theyll actually react physicly correct to how you interacted with them.

There are 10 Levels in the game. That are all pretty big. So there is no pre-determined way to go like in call of duty. Each of the levels are several square kilometers big that you can actually walk on. And there aren't really any areas that feel empty.

The AI is pretty smart for the most part. On the highest difficulty they are pretty hard to beat at times. However they aren't perfect ofcourse either. For instance in the 1st level there is a guy in a toilet. and 8/10 times when he gets alert to you he runs into the wall of the toilet instead of out through the door.

The Story is probably the games weakest feature, which doesn't say it's bad. It's just nothing particularly special either. That beeing said, as a little side note: The story in Crysis 2 is actually quiet an improvement over the one in Crysis 1.

And now the most important gameplay element: The nanosuit. For me this made it for one super cool, cause you are some super hero kind badass (with a slightly more grounded background lore to how the powers work than most comic book super heroes). And also I think it makes for some very fun options gameplay wise. You have great mobility with speed and strength mode. you can choose to fight as a tank with armor mode (although you still die very quick on delta difficulty so its not crazy overpowered) and you can play very stealthy with the cloak mode (which makes you almost but not completly invisible).
All those abilities use the suit's energy, so they can not be used indefinitly.
And the best thing is you can switch in between the diffrent suitmodes at any time, so you can adapt your playstyle to the situation at any given time.

Last: The Multiplayer:
So appereantly the multiplayer doesn't work anymore due to the service it used (gamespy) shutting down. However there may be workarounds to still play online. And the LAN mode still works ofcourse.
I personally didn't bother much with the multiplayer in crysis 1. Back when I tried it it seemed alright, but I don't think it lived auiet up to the potential of multiplayer fun there could have been with the nanosuit. crysis 2 was an improvement in that regard in my opinion.

So all in all Crysis 1(and I'm mainly referring to the singleplayer here) in my opinion is one of the best shooters ever made. And I'd recommend it to anyone who hasn't played it yet. (9/10) (10/10 if you choose to ignore the slightly weaker story)

Never having played the famous Crysis, I thought I'd finally give it a shot and find out what the fuss is all about. Naturally, since I played this in 2014, my perspective on the game will be very different from the one who played it when it came out. But only an hour into the game, I realized why people call it such a revolutionary shooter for its time. I didn't play with any mods, yet I would've never guessed the game I was playing came out in 2007 judging from what it presented to me. This is due to the following reasons:

- The vastness of the world and the graphical fidelity are overwhelmingly impressive for an FPS title this old. You can clearly see that the CryEngine is designed to push the limits on what's possible in terms of looks and scope. I was impressed by how open-world-y the terrain is, yet the missions are unmistakably straightforward... which turns out to be an incredibly fun combination in my opinion. Being dropped on a tropical island where you shoot people in a vast and open area offering multiple ways of approaching your goals is to my mind a great way to design an FPS. The level of detail is stunning to say the least for a 2007 title, I have seen much worse in considerably newer titles.

- The gunplay, gun variety and AI are simply great. Shooting enemies feels fun, feels rewarding and feels challenging since the AI actively tries to hunt you down when you for example sneaked away again using cloak. One of the core mechanics, the exosuit and its accompanying suit powers offer great variety for both people who like to be stealthy or those who love to cause mayhem. I found a mix of these to be the most effective and entertaining. Goddamnit I think I never experienced as much satisfaction as when I blew up a truck with a rocket launcher while crouching in a bush with cloak engaged. The effects are mindblowing, as are the sound assets, just really immersive overall.

- Performance is solid. With CFX 7950/7970 I easily manage 60fps, except for very intense scenes involving lots of explosions and stuff. FoV seems to be exceptionally high, I didn't see a slider for it in the menu, but it's at least 100 by default, which is great. Sadly there's a few bugs involving for example scripted events and cutscenes not triggering correctly when loading from quicksaves amidst a level, nothing game-breaking though. Also, 1920x1080 or higher resolution is not enabled by default, you have to manually adjust it in the config file, which is no big deal though.

- The level design is interesting enough. While most levels feature open tropical island terrain with hilly, foresty areas, there's also a sequence where you are in weightless space, floating around inside a gigantic alien structure; very impressive and intriguing overall. The enemy variety is great too: From your usual infantry of all kind to jeeps, tanks, helicopters, boats to rather pesky flying alien crystalline squids with fast-firing energy weapons to a huge ass alien motherfugger in the process of sinking a motherfuggin aircraft carrier. It should be noted that you can drive jeeps, tanks, boats and helicopters yourself which is super fun if you like to shoot up stuff in the most classy way imaginable.

Negative points? I have one major one, but perhaps it's not really valid since the game clearly doesn't focus on that aspect at all and never pretends to:

The story is mindblowingly clichée and superficial: >Technologically augmented super soldier infiltrates fictional island under the control of evil North Koreans, gathers intel, blows up stuff, uncovers archeological project gone overboard, sleeping alien entity that feeds itself off energy awakens, causes major destruction, gruffy American general wants to drop nuke on island to kill off the monstrosity, super-intelligent scientists who always know it better advise against it, alien gets nuked anyway, becomes massively stronger, protagonist has to beat XXL format version of alien monstrosity using lots of missiles and a super secret prototype weapon which had never been field-tested but works like a charm (why wouldn't it?), escapes a sinking aircraft carrier and goes right back into the fight because he's a badass and a superhuman, dutiful soldier-tough-guy who has no fear and throughout the entire game requires no sleep at all. 
There, that's the plot in a nutshell for you. Not really intentended in the beginning but hey, these are spontaneous and minimally structured reviews after all so w/e. 
So there you go, awesome FPS, don't play it for the story, play it for the mechanics and the looks. This is how every modern military shooter should be. You can make a very linear, bland narrative without sacrificing diversity and creativity in terms of gameplay and mechanics. Crysis taught us this. 

No score here, read the damn review if you care for my opinion on it.

Ah, Crysis, sort of a tech demo and sort of a game. This is not the remastered version, but the original, but then, the remastered version is designed to melt MODERN video cards. It's beautiful, and flexible enough to make things... interesting, and probably what really put "sandbox shooter" genre on the map. 

The plot is sort of cliche and sort of isn't. In 2020, a US science team sent out a mayday... North Koreans are invading Lingshan Island off the Phillippines. US, not wanting to raise tensions, sent in Raptor Team, an elite group of US Special Forces equipped with the latest generation nano-suits that can enhance speed, strength, armor, or even go stealth, for limited time. But something else is on the island... as the team dives, members are picked off by strange flying creatures. Only 3 landed successfully, Prophet was subsequently lost, another, Psycho, had his own mission (playable as Crysis:Warhead)  Only Nomad (you), is left to complete the mission... What is the North Korean up to? Who/what are those flying creatures? What had humanity gotten itself into this time? 

Obviously you had to explore the island, deal with various types of threats using both conventional and improved weapons. But your suit also has various modes you can exploit. Toss a tank at the enemy soldiers? Definitely possible. Sneak up behind him and knife him? Can be done. Tactical possibilities are endless, given your expanded toolset. 

Obviously, your enemies are tougher too. Lots of NK soldiers around, and later, yes, you'll meet some tougher opponents... and THEN there are the unexpected opponents. And let's just say, things don't go well. 

Graphics were phenomenal for the time, and requires a VERY hefty PC to run at the time. It's too bad that Crytek has gotten out of AAA-title business altogether. And the story line is not bad, even if it went for more scifi cliche tropes in the two sequels. 

Should you play it? Absolutely. Even if it's not the remastered version.
